## About

I'm a PhD candidate in Economic History at Lund University, defending in Spring 2026. **I study how innovation emerges—and who gets to innovate.**

My research builds large-scale patent and inventor microdata (390,000 French patents, 255,000 unique inventors, 1791–1900) to explain the gender patenting gap, trace how collaboration reshapes inventors' careers, and measure the diffusion of ideas. I develop machine-learning pipelines—Computer Vision for handwritten archives, fine-tuned transformer models, and probabilistic record linkage—to transform historical records into analyzable data.

I'm supervised by [Faustine Perrin](https://portal.research.lu.se/en/persons/faustine-perrin) and [Josef Taalbi](https://portal.research.lu.se/en/persons/josef-taalbi).

For more, see my [research](research/index.qmd), [talks](talks.qmd), [teaching](teaching.qmd), [dissertation introduction](research/working_papers/Merouani-Dissertation-Kappa.pdf), and [CV](Youssouf_Merouani_shortCV.pdf).

<p></p>

## Job Market Paper

**What Happens When Inventors Collaborate? Evidence from 19th-Century French Patents**  
Merouani, Y. 2026. [[Draft PDF]](research/working_papers/Merouani-Patent-Collaboration-Networks.pdf)

Using text-based measures of novelty and influence and Sun–Abraham event studies on the full universe of French patents, I show that collaboration does not raise productivity or originality—but permanently diversifies inventors' technological focus. Network analysis reveals that "structural holes" enable this boundary-crossing, with particularly strong effects for women inventors.

<p></p>
